HISTORICAL COMMENTS One topic among many important ones in this chapter is regression, a technique that leads to a mathematical model of the result of some process in terms of some associated (explanatory) variables. We create such models to give us some idea of the value of a response variable if we know the values of certain explanatory variables. If we have an idea of the form of the equation relating these variables, then we can “fit” this model to the data; that is, we can determine approximate values for the unknown parameters in the model from the data. Now, no model is exactly correct, but, as the well-known statistician George Box observed, “Some are useful.” That is, while models may be wrong and we should check them as best we can, they may be good enough approximations to shed some light on the issues of interest. 

Once satisfactory models are found, they may be used 

1. To determine the effect of each explanatory variable (some may have very little effect and can be dropped), 

2. To estimate the conditional mean of the response variable for given values of important explanatory variables, 

3. To predict the future, such as upcoming sales (although this sometimes should be done with great care), 

4. To often substitute a cheaper explanatory variable for an expensive one that is difficult to obtain [such as chemical oxygen demand (COD) for biological oxygen demand (BOD)]. 

The name bootstrap and the resulting technique were first used by Brad Efron of Stanford University. Efron knew that the expression “to pull oneself up by his or her own bootstraps” seems to come from The Surprising Adventures of Baron Munchausen by Rudolph Erich Raspe. The baron had fallen from the sky and found himself in a hole nine fathoms deep and had no idea how to get out. He comments as follows: “Looking down I observed that I had on a pair of boots with exceptionally sturdy straps. Grasping them firmly, I pulled with all my might. Soon I had hoisted myself to the top and stepped out on terra firma without further ado.” 

Of course, in statistical bootstrapping, statisticians pull themselves up by their bootstraps (the empirical distributions) by recognizing that the empirical distribution is the best estimate of the underlying distribution without a lot of other assumptions. So they use the empirical distribution as if it is the underlying distribution to find approximate distributions of statistics of interest.

## 8.1 TESTS ABOUT ONE MEAN

Interval estimation of a parameter using a confidence interval, as described in the previous chapter, is one important form of statistical inference. Another is hypothesis testing. For hypothesis testing, it is assumed that the parameter θ of a distribution lies in a parameter space , which can be partitioned into two nonoverlapping disjoint subsets $\Theta _ { 0 }$ and $\Theta _ { 1 }$ . The statistical problem of interest is to use the observed data to decide whether $\theta ~ \in ~ \Theta _ { 0 }$ , called the null hypothesis and written as $H _ { 0 } \colon \theta \ \in \ \Theta _ { 0 }$ , or $\theta \in \Theta _ { 1 }$ , called the alternative hypothesis and written as $H _ { 1 } \colon \theta \ \in \ \Theta _ { 1 }$ . The particular way in which the data are used to decide between the two competing hypotheses is called a hypothesis testing procedure, or more simply, a test. Describing tests about certain parameters and characterizing some of their properties are the subjects of this chapter. 

We begin with an application of hypothesis testing to the mean $\mu$ of a single population, in which we define many of the terms associated with testing. 

Let X equal the breaking strength of a steel bar. If the bar is manufactured by process I, X is N(50, 36). It is hoped that if process II (a new process) is used, X will be N(55, 36). Given a large number of steel bars manufactured by process II, how could we test whether the five-unit increase in the mean breaking strength was realized? 

In this problem, we are assuming that X is $N ( \mu , 3 6 )$ and $\mu$ is equal to either 50 or 55. We want to test the simple null hypothesis H : $\mu = 5 0$ against the simple alternative hypothesis $H _ { 1 } \colon \mu = 5 5$ . Note that each of these hypotheses completely specifies the distribution of X, which is why they are called simple. That is, $H _ { 0 }$ states that X is N(50, 36) and $H _ { 1 }$ states that X is N(55, 36). (If the alternative hypothesis had been $H _ { 1 } \colon \mu > 5 0$ , it would be a composite hypothesis, because it is composed of all normal distributions with $\sigma ^ { 2 } = 3 6$ and means greater than 50.) In order to test which of the two hypotheses, $H _ { 0 }$ or $H _ { 1 }$ , is true, we shall set up a rule based on the breaking strengths $x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , \ldots , x _ { n }$ of n bars (the observed values of a random sample of size n). The rule leads to a decision to reject or fail to reject $H _ { 0 } ;$ hence, it is necessary to partition the sample space into two parts—say, C and $C ^ { \prime } { - } { \bf s } { \bf o }$ that if $( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , \ldots , x _ { n } ) \in$ $C , H _ { 0 }$ is rejected, and if $( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , \ldots , x _ { n } ) \in C ^ { \prime } , H _ { 0 }$ is not rejected. The rejection region C for $H _ { 0 }$ is called the critical region for the test. Often, the partitioning of the sample space is specified in terms of the values of a statistic called the test statistic. In this example, we could let $\overline { { X } }$ be the test statistic and, say, take $C = \{ ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , \ldots , x _ { n } ) \colon { \overline { { x } } } \geq$ 53}; that is, we will reject $H _ { 0 } { \mathrm { ~ i f ~ } } { \overline { { x } } } \geq 5 3$ . If $( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , \ldots , x _ { n } ) \in C$ when $H _ { 0 }$ is true, $H _ { 0 }$ would be rejected when it is true, a Type I error. If $( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } , \ldots , x _ { n } ) \in C ^ { \prime }$ when $H _ { 1 }$ is true, we would not reject $H _ { 0 }$ when in fact $H _ { 1 }$ is true, thereby committing a Type II error. The probability of a Type I error is called the significance level of the test and is denoted by $\alpha .$ That is, $\alpha = P [ ( X _ { 1 } , X _ { 2 } , \ldots , X _ { n } ) \in C ; H _ { 0 } ]$ is the probability that $( X _ { 1 } , X _ { 2 } , \ldots , X _ { n } )$ falls into C when $H _ { 0 }$ is true. The probability of a Type II error is denoted by β; that is, $\beta = P [ ( X _ { 1 } , X _ { 2 } , \ldots , X _ { n } ) \in C ^ { \prime } ; H _ { 1 } ]$ is the probability of failing to reject $H _ { 0 }$ when it is false. 

As an illustration, suppose $n = 1 6$ bars were tested and $C = \{ \overline { { x } } : \overline { { x } } \geq 5 3 \}$ . Then $\overline { { X } }$ is N(50, 36/16) when $H _ { 0 }$ is true and is N(55, 36/16) when $H _ { 1 }$ is true. Thus, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \alpha = P (\overline {{X}} \geq 5 3; H _ {0}) = P \left(\frac {\overline {{X}} - 5 0}{6 / 4} \geq \frac {5 3 - 5 0}{6 / 4}; H _ {0}\right) \\ = 1 - \Phi (2) = 0. 0 2 2 8 \end{array}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \beta = P (\overline {{{X}}} <   5 3; H _ {1}) = P \left(\frac {\overline {{{X}}} - 5 5}{6 / 4} <   \frac {5 3 - 5 5}{6 / 4}; H _ {1}\right) \\ = \Phi \left(- \frac {4}{3}\right) = 1 - 0. 9 0 8 7 = 0. 0 9 1 3. \end{array}
$$

Figure 8.1-1 shows the graphs of the probability density functions of $\overline { { X } }$ when $H _ { 0 }$ and $H _ { 1 }$ , respectively, are true. Note that a decrease in the size of α leads to an increase in the size of $\beta _ { ; }$ , and vice versa. Both α and $\beta$ can be decreased if the sample size n is increased. 

Through another example, we define a $p \mathrm { - }$ -value obtained in testing a hypothesis about a mean. 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-11-17/1c33a83b-ce50-427b-ab88-165fc0cc3d67/345cd0eb77efa519bcf197ef71c8d72b630de33ba2a7b67259886cd16555972b.jpg)



Figure 8.1-1 pdf of $\overline { { X } }$ under $H _ { 0 }$ and $H _ { 1 }$


Assume that the underlying distribution is normal with unknown mean $\mu$ but known variance $\sigma ^ { 2 } = 1 0 0 ^ { \circ }$ . Say we are testing the simple null hypothesis $H _ { 0 } ; \mu = 6 0$ against the composite alternative hypothesis $H _ { 1 } \colon \mu > 6 0$ with a sample mean $\overline { { X } }$ based on $n = 5 2$ observations. Suppose that we obtain the observed sample mean of $\overline { { x } } = 6 2 . 7 5$ If we compute the probability of obtaining an $\overline { { X } }$ of that value of 62.75 or greater when $\mu = 6 0$ , then we obtain the p-value associated with $\overline { { x } } = 6 2 . 7 5$ . That is, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} p \text {-value} = P (\overline {{X}} \geq 6 2. 7 5; \mu = 6 0) \\ \quad = P \left(\frac {\overline {{X}} - 6 0}{1 0 / \sqrt {5 2}} \geq \frac {6 2 . 7 5 - 6 0}{1 0 / \sqrt {5 2}}; \mu = 6 0\right) \\ \quad = 1 - \Phi \left(\frac {6 2 . 7 5 - 6 0}{1 0 / \sqrt {5 2}}\right) = 1 - \Phi (1. 9 8 3) = 0. 0 2 3 7. \end{array}
$$

If this p-value is small, we tend to reject the hypothesis $H _ { 0 } \colon \mu = 6 0$ . For example, rejecting H<sub>0</sub>: $\mu = 6 0$ if the p-value is less than or equal to $\alpha = 0 . 0 5$ is exactly the same as rejecting $H _ { 0 }$ if 

$$
\bar {x} \geq 6 0 + (1. 6 4 5) \left(\frac {1 0}{\sqrt {5 2}}\right) = 6 2. 2 8 1.
$$

Here 

$$
p \text {-value} = 0. 0 2 3 7 <   \alpha = 0. 0 5 \quad \text { and } \quad \overline {{x}} = 6 2. 7 5 > 6 2. 2 8 1.
$$

To help the reader keep the definition of p-value in mind, we note that it can be thought of as the tail-end probability, under $H _ { 0 } ,$ of the distribution of the statistic (here $\overline { { X } } )$ beyond the observed value of the statistic. (See Figure 8.1-2 for the $p \cdot$ -value associated with $\overline { { x } } = 6 2 . 7 5 .$ ) 1 

In general, the p-value associated with any hypothesis test for a single parameter is the probability, under the null hypothesis, that the test statistic is at least as extreme as its observed value. Here, “extreme" is taken to mean “away from $H _ { 0 }$ in the direction(s) of $H _ { 1 }$ ." Thus, if a one-sided $H _ { 1 }$ consists entirely of values that lie to the right of the parameter’s value under $H _ { 0 }$ (as was the case in Example 8.1-2), then thep-value is the probability, computed as if the random experiment has not yet been performed, that the test statistic lies to the right of its observed value. A similar statement applies if $H _ { 1 }$ is one-sided and consists entirely of values that lie to the left of the parameter’s value under $H _ { 0 }$ . If $H _ { 1 }$ is two-sided, then the test statistic is regarded as extreme if it is either too large or too small. Accordingly, the $p \mathrm { - }$ value associated with a two-sided test is generally taken to equal twice the smaller of the probability that the test statistic is greater than or equal to its observed value and the probability that it is less than or equal to its observed value. Thus, if the alternative hypothesis in Example 8.1-2 had been the two-sided $H _ { 1 } \colon \mu \ne 6 0$ , then the $p \cdot$ -value would have been $2 ( 0 . 0 2 3 7 ) = 0 . 0 4 7 4$

Figure 8.1-2 Illustration of p-value


The p-value, as just defined, is a data-based measure of the truth of $H _ { 0 } \colon$ the smaller the p-value, the less we believe in $H _ { 0 }$ . As such, it conveys more information than a statement such as $^ { * } H _ { 0 }$ is rejected at the α level of significance" for a specific choice of $\alpha ,$ , as this statement doesn’t indicate whether $H _ { 0 }$ would be rejected at other choices of $\alpha .$ Accordingly, most scientific researchers using statistical hypothesis tests report p-values. 

When we sample from a normal distribution, the null hypothesis is generally of the form $H _ { 0 } \colon \mu = \mu _ { 0 }$ . There are three possibilities of interest for a composite alternative hypothesis: (i) that $\mu$ has increased, or $H _ { 1 } \colon \mu > \mu _ { 0 } ; ( \mathrm { i i } )$ that $\mu$ has decreased, or $H _ { 1 } \colon \mu < \mu _ { 0 } ;$ and (iii) that $\mu$ has changed, but it is not known whether it has increased or decreased, which leads to the two-sided alternative hypothesis, or $H _ { 1 } \colon \mu \neq \mu _ { 0 }$ 

To test $H _ { 0 } \colon \mu = \mu _ { 0 }$ against one of these three alternative hypotheses, a random sample is taken from the distribution and an observed sample mean, x, that is close to $\mu _ { 0 }$ supports $H _ { 0 }$ . The closeness o $\mathit { \Pi } _ { : \overline { { x } } }$ to $\mu _ { 0 }$ is measured in terms of standard deviations of ${ \overline { { X } } } , { \bar { \sigma } } / { \sqrt { n } }$ , when $\sigma$ is known, a measure that is sometimes called the standard error of the mean. Thus, the test statistic could be defined by 

$$
Z = \frac {\overline {{X}} - \mu_ {0}}{\sqrt {\sigma^ {2} / n}} = \frac {\overline {{X}} - \mu_ {0}}{\sigma / \sqrt {n}},\tag{8.1-1}
$$

and the critical regions, at a significance level $\alpha ,$ for the three respective alternative hypotheses would be $\mathrm { ( i ) } z \geq z _ { \alpha } , \mathrm { ( i i ) } z \leq - z _ { \alpha }$ , and $\mathrm { ( i i i ) } \ | z | \geq z _ { \alpha / 2 }$ . In terms of ${ \overline { { x } } } ,$ these three critical regions become $( \mathrm { i } ) { \overline { { x } } } \geq \mu _ { 0 } + z _ { \alpha } ( \sigma / { \sqrt { n } } ) , ( \mathrm { i i } ) { \overline { { x } } } \leq \mu _ { 0 } - z _ { \alpha } ( \sigma / { \sqrt { n } } )$ , and (iii) $| \overline { { x } } - \mu _ { 0 } | \geq z _ { \alpha / 2 } ( \sigma / \sqrt { n } )$ 

The three tests and critical regions are summarized in Table 8.1-1. The underlying assumptions are that the distribution is $N ( \mu , \sigma ^ { 2 } )$ and $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ is known. 

It is usually the case in practice that the variance $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ is not known. Accordingly, we now take a more realistic position and assume that the variance is unknown. Suppose our null hypothesis is H<sub>0</sub>: $\mu = \mu _ { 0 }$ and the two-sided alternative hypothesis is $H _ { 1 }$ : $\mu \neq \mu _ { 0 }$ . Recall from Section 7.1 that for a random sample $X _ { 1 } , X _ { 2 } , \ldots , X _ { n }$ taken from a normal distribution $N ( \mu , \sigma ^ { 2 } )$ , a confidence interval for $\mu$ may be based on 


Table 8.1-1 Tests of hypotheses about one mean, variance known


<table><tr><td><eq>H_0</eq></td><td><eq>H_1</eq></td><td>Critical Region</td></tr><tr><td><eq>\mu = \mu_0</eq></td><td><eq>\mu &gt;\mu_0</eq></td><td><eq>z \geq z_\alpha \text{ or } \overline{x} \geq \mu_0 + z_\alpha \sigma/\sqrt{n}</eq></td></tr><tr><td><eq>\mu = \mu_0</eq></td><td><eq>\mu &lt; \mu_0</eq></td><td><eq>z \leq -z_\alpha \text{ or } \overline{x} \leq \mu_0 - z_\alpha \sigma/\sqrt{n}</eq></td></tr><tr><td><eq>\mu = \mu_0</eq></td><td><eq>\mu \neq \mu_0</eq></td><td><eq>|z| \geq z_{\alpha/2} \text{ or } |\overline{x} - \mu_0| \geq z_{\alpha/2} \sigma/\sqrt{n}</eq></td></tr></table>

$$
T = \frac {\overline {{X}} - \mu}{\sqrt {S ^ {2} / n}} = \frac {\overline {{X}} - \mu}{S / \sqrt {n}}.
$$

This suggests that T might be a good statistic to use for the test of $H _ { 0 } \colon \mu = \mu _ { 0 }$ with $\mu$ replaced by $\mu _ { 0 } .$ . In addition, it is the natural statistic to use if we replace $\sigma ^ { 2 } / n$ by its unbiased estimator $S ^ { 2 } / n$ in $( \overline { { X } } - \mu _ { 0 } ) / \sqrt { \sigma ^ { 2 } / n }$ in Equation 8.1-1. If $\mu = \mu _ { 0 }$ , we know that T has a t distribution with $n - 1$ degrees of freedom. Thus, with $\mu = \mu _ { 0 }$ 

$$
P [ | T | \geq t _ {\alpha / 2} (n - 1) ] = P \left[ \frac {| \overline {{X}} - \mu_ {0} |}{S / \sqrt {n}} \geq t _ {\alpha / 2} (n - 1) \right] = \alpha .
$$

Accordingly, if x and s are, respectively, the sample mean and sample standard deviation, then the rule that rejects H<sub>0</sub>: $\mu = \mu _ { 0 }$ if and only if 

$$
| t | = \frac {| \overline {{x}} - \mu_ {0} |}{s / \sqrt {n}} \geq t _ {\alpha / 2} (n - 1)
$$

provides a test of this hypothesis with significance level α. Note that this rule is equivalent to rejecting H<sub>0</sub>: $\mu ~ = ~ \mu _ { 0 }$ if $\mu _ { 0 }$ is not in the open $1 0 0 ( 1 - \alpha ) \%$ confidence interval 

$$
(\overline {{x}} - t _ {\alpha / 2} (n - 1) (s / \sqrt {n}),   \overline {{x}} + t _ {\alpha / 2} (n - 1) (s / \sqrt {n})).
$$

Table 8.1-2 summarizes tests of hypotheses for a single mean along with the three possible alternative hypotheses when the underlying distribution is $\mathbf { \bar { \boldsymbol { N } } } ( \mu , \sigma ^ { 2 } ) , \sigma ^ { 2 }$ is unknown, $t \ = \ ( \overline { { x } } - \mu _ { 0 } ) / ( s / \sqrt { n } )$ , and $n ~ \leq ~ 3 0 .$ . If $n \ > \ 3 0 .$ , we use Table 8.1-1 for approximate tests, with σ replaced by s. 

Let X (in millimeters) equal the growth in 15 days of a tumor induced in a mouse. Assume that the distribution of $X$ is $N ( \mu , \sigma ^ { 2 } )$ . We shall test the null hypothesis $H _ { 0 } \colon$ $\mu = \mu _ { 0 } = 4 . 0$ mm against the two-sided alternative hypothesis $H _ { 1 } \colon \mu \neq 4 . 0 .$ . If we use $n = 9$ observations and a significance level of $\alpha = 0 . 1 0$ , the critical region is 

$$
| t | = \frac {| \overline {{{x}}} - 4 . 0 |}{s / \sqrt {9}} \geq t _ {\alpha / 2} (8) = 1. 8 6 0.
$$

If we are given that $n = 9 , { \overline { { x } } } = 4 . 3$ , and $s = 1 . 2$ , we see that 

$$
t = \frac {4 . 3 - 4 . 0}{1 . 2 / \sqrt {9}} = \frac {0 . 3}{0 . 4} = 0. 7 5.
$$

Thus, 

$$
| t | = | 0. 7 5 | <   1. 8 6 0,
$$

and we do not reject $H _ { 0 } ; \mu = 4 . 0$ at the $\alpha = 1 0 \%$ significance level. (See Figure 8.1-3.) The p-value is the two-sided probability of $| T | \ge 0 . 7 5$ , namely, 

$$
p \text {-value} = P (| T | \geq 0. 7 5) = 2 P (T \geq 0. 7 5).
$$

With our t tables with eight degrees of freedom, we cannot find this p-value exactly. It is about 0.50 because 

$$
P (| T | \geq 0. 7 0 6) = 2 P (T \geq 0. 7 0 6) = 0. 5 0.
$$

However, Minitab gives a p-value of 0.4747. (See Figure 8.1-3.) 

The next example illustrates the use of the t statistic with a one-sided alternative hypothesis. 

In attempting to control the strength of the wastes discharged into a nearby river, a paper firm has taken a number of measures. Members of the firm believe that they have reduced the oxygen-consuming power of their wastes from a previous mean μ of 500 (measured in parts per million of permanganate). They plan to test $H _ { 0 } \colon \mu = 5 0 0$ against $H _ { 1 } \colon \mu \ < \ 5 0 0$ , using readings taken on $n = 2 5$ consecutive days. If these 25 values can be treated as a random sample, then the critical region, for a significance level of $\alpha = 0 . 0 1$ , is 

$$
t = \frac {\overline {{x}} - 5 0 0}{s / \sqrt {2 5}} \leq - t _ {0. 0 1} (2 4) = - 2. 4 9 2.
$$

The observed values of the sample mean and sample standard deviation were ${ \overline { { x } } } =$ 308.8 and $s = 1 1 5 . 1 5$ . Because 

$$
t = \frac {3 0 8 . 8 - 5 0 0}{1 1 5 . 1 5 / \sqrt {2 5}} = - 8. 3 0 <   - 2. 4 9 2,
$$

we clearly reject the null hypothesis. Note, however, that although an improvement has been made, there still might exist the question of whether the improvement is adequate. The one-sided 99% confidence interval for $\mu ,$ , namely, 

$$
[ 0, 3 0 8. 8 + 2. 4 9 2 (1 1 5. 2 5 / \sqrt {2 5}) ] = [ 0, 3 6 6. 1 9 1 ],
$$

provides an upper bound for $\mu$ and may help the company answer this question. 

There is often an equivalence between hypothesis tests and confidence intervals. For example, with the mouse data (Example 8.1-3), a 90% confidence interval for the unknown mean is 

$$
4. 3 \pm (1. 8 6) (1. 2) / \sqrt {9}, \quad \text { or } \quad [ 3. 5 6, 5. 0 4 ],
$$

because $t _ { 0 . 0 5 } ( 8 ) = 1 . 8 6$ . Note that this confidence interval covers the hypothesized value $\mu = 4 . 0$ and we do not reject H<sub>0</sub>: $\mu = 4 . 0$ . If the confidence interval did not cover $\mu = 4 . 0$ , then we would have rejected $H _ { 0 } \colon \mu = 4 . 0$ . Many statisticians believe that estimation is much more important than tests of hypotheses and accordingly approach statistical tests through confidence intervals. For one-sided tests, we use one-sided confidence intervals.

## 8.2 TESTS OF THE EQUALITY OF TWO MEANS

Oftentimes, there is interest in comparing the means of two different distributions or populations. We must consider two situations according to whether the observations from the two populations arise from paired sampling or independent sampling. We consider the paired sampling case first. 

If X and Y are sampled using paired sampling, then we may let $D = X - Y ,$ and the hypothesis that $\mu _ { X } = \mu _ { Y }$ may be replaced with the equivalent hypothesis $H _ { 0 } \colon$ $\mu _ { D } = 0 .$ . For example, suppose that X and Y equal the resting pulse rate for a person before and after taking an eight-week program in aerobic dance. We would be interested in testing $H _ { 0 } \colon \mu _ { D } = 0$ (no change) against $H _ { 1 } \colon \mu _ { D } > 0$ (the aerobic dance program decreased the resting pulse rate). Because X and Y are measurements on the same person, X and Y are likely to be dependent. If we can assume that the distribution of D is (approximately) $N ( \mu _ { D } , \sigma _ { D } ^ { 2 } )$ , then we can choose to use the appropriate t test for a single mean from Table 8.1-2. This is often called a paired t test. 

Twenty-four girls in the ninth and tenth grades were put on an ultraheavy ropejumping program. Someone thought that such a program would increase their speed in the 40-yard dash. Let D equal the difference in time to run the 40-yard dash—the “before-program time” minus the “after-program time.” Assume that the distribution of D is approximately $N ( \mu _ { D } , \sigma _ { D } ^ { 2 } )$ . We shall test the null hypothesis $H _ { 0 } \colon \mu _ { D } = 0$ against the alternative hypothesis $H _ { 1 } \colon \mu _ { D } > 0$ . The test statistic and the critical region that has an $\alpha = 0 . 0 5$ significance level are given by 

$$
t = \frac {\overline {{d}} - 0}{s _ {D} / \sqrt {2 4}} \geq t _ {0. 0 5} (2 3) = 1. 7 1 4.
$$

The following data give the difference in time that it took each girl to run the 40-yard dash, with positive numbers indicating a faster time after the program: 

$$
\begin{array}{r r r r r r r r} 0. 2 8 & 0. 0 1 & 0. 1 3 & 0. 3 3 & - 0. 0 3 & 0. 0 7 & - 0. 1 8 & - 0. 1 4 \\ - 0. 3 3 & 0. 0 1 & 0. 2 2 & 0. 2 9 & - 0. 0 8 & 0. 2 3 & 0. 0 8 & 0. 0 4 \\ - 0. 3 0 & - 0. 0 8 & 0. 0 9 & 0. 7 0 & 0. 3 3 & - 0. 3 4 & 0. 5 0 & 0. 0 6 \end{array}
$$

For these data, $\overline { { d } } \ : = \ : 0 . 0 7 9$ and $s _ { D } ~ = ~ 0 . 2 5 5$ . Thus, the observed value of the test statistic is 

$$
t = \frac {0 . 0 7 9 - 0}{0 . 2 5 5 / \sqrt {2 4}} = 1. 5 1 8.
$$

Because 1.518 < 1.714, the null hypothesis is not rejected. Note, however, that $t _ { 0 . 1 0 } ( 2 3 ) = 1 . 3 1 9$ and $t = 1 . 5 1 8 > 1 . 3 1 9$ . Hence, the null hypothesis would be rejected at an α = 0.10 significance level. Another way of saying this is that 

$$
0. 0 5 <   p \text {-value} <   0. 1 0.
$$

Now suppose that the random variables X and Y are independently sampled, and that they have normal distributions $N ( \mu _ { X } , \sigma _ { X } ^ { 2 } )$ and $N ( \mu _ { Y } , \hat { \sigma } _ { Y } ^ { 2 } )$ . We wish to test the null hypothesis $H _ { 0 } \colon \mu _ { X } = \mu _ { Y }$ against the alternative hypothesis $H _ { 1 } \colon \mu _ { X } \neq \mu _ { Y }$ (or possibly against either one of the one-sided alternatives $\mu _ { X } < \mu _ { Y }$ or $\mu _ { X } > \mu _ { Y } )$ . We can test these types of hypotheses using a t-distributed quantity similar to the one we used to construct a confidence interval for $\mu _ { X } - \mu _ { Y }$ in Section 7.2. 

When X and Y are independent and normally distributed, we can test hypotheses about their means with the same t statistic that we used to construct a confidence interval for $\mu _ { X } - \mu _ { Y }$ in Section 7.2. Recall that the t-distributed quantity used to construct the confidence interval assumed that the variances of X and Y were equal. (That is why we shall consider a test for the equality of two variances in the next section.) 

We begin with an example and then give a table that lists some hypotheses and critical regions. A botanist is interested in comparing the growth response of dwarf pea stems against two different levels of the hormone indoleacetic acid (IAA). Using 16-day-old pea plants, the botanist obtains 5-mm sections and floats these sections on solutions with different hormone concentrations to observe the effect of the hormone on the growth of the pea stem. Let X and Y denote, respectively, the independent growths that can be attributed to the hormone during the first 26 hours after sectioning for $( 0 . 5 ) ( 1 0 ) ^ { - 4 }$ and $1 0 ^ { - 4 }$ levels of concentration of IAA. The botanist would like to test the null hypothesis $H _ { 0 } \colon \mu _ { X } - \mu _ { Y } = 0$ against the alternative hypothesis $H _ { 1 } \colon \mu _ { X } - \mu _ { Y } < 0$ . If we can assume that X and Y are independent and normally distributed with a common variance, and if we assume respective random samples of sizes $n _ { X }$ and $n _ { Y }$ , then we can find a test based on the statistic 

$$
\begin{array}{l} T = \frac {\overline {{X}} - \overline {{Y}}}{\sqrt {\left\{\left[ (n _ {X} - 1) S _ {X} ^ {2} + (n _ {Y} - 1) S _ {Y} ^ {2} \right] / (n _ {X} + n _ {Y} - 2) \right\} (1 / n _ {X} + 1 / n _ {Y})}} \\ = \frac {\overline {{X}} - \overline {{Y}}}{S _ {P} \sqrt {1 / n _ {X} + 1 / n _ {Y}}}, \end{array}\tag{8.2-1}
$$

where 

$$
S _ {P} = \sqrt {\frac {(n _ {X} - 1) S _ {X} ^ {2} + (n _ {Y} - 1) S _ {Y} ^ {2}}{n _ {X} + n _ {Y} - 2}}.\tag{8.2-2}
$$

Now, T has a t distribution with $r = n _ { X } + n _ { Y } - 2$ degrees of freedom when $H _ { 0 }$ is true. Thus, the hypothesis $H _ { 0 }$ will be rejected in favor of $H _ { 1 }$ if the observed value of $T$ is less than or equal $\mathrm { t o } - t _ { \alpha } ( n _ { X } + n _ { Y } - 2 )$ 

In the preceding discussion, the botanist measured the growths of pea stem segments in millimeters for $n _ { X } = 1 1$ observations of X: 

$$
\begin{array}{l l l l l l l l l l l} 0. 8 & 1. 8 & 1. 0 & 0. 1 & 0. 9 & 1. 7 & 1. 0 & 1. 4 & 0. 9 & 1. 2 & 0. 5 \end{array}
$$

She did the same with $n _ { Y } = 1 3$ observations of $Y \colon$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c c c c c c c} 1. 0 & 0. 8 & 1. 6 & 2. 6 & 1. 3 & 1. 1 & 2. 4 \\ 1. 8 & 2. 5 & 1. 4 & 1. 9 & 2. 0 & 1. 2 \end{array}
$$

For these data, $\overline { { x } } = 1 . 0 3 , s _ { \scriptscriptstyle X } ^ { 2 } = 0 . 2 4 , \overline { { y } } = 1 . 6 6$ , and $s _ { Y } ^ { 2 } = 0 . 3 5$ . The critical region for testing $H _ { 0 } ; \mu _ { X } - \mu _ { Y } = 0$ against $H _ { 1 } ; \mu _ { X } - \mu _ { Y } < 0$ is $t \le - t _ { 0 . 0 5 } ( 2 2 ) = - 1 . 7 1 7$ , where t is the two-sample t found in Equation 8.2-1. Because 

$$
\begin{array}{l} t = \frac {1 . 0 3 - 1 . 6 6}{\sqrt {\{[ 1 0 (0 . 2 4) + 1 2 (0 . 3 5) ] / (1 1 + 1 3 - 2) \} (1 / 1 1 + 1 / 1 3)}} \\ = - 2. 8 1 <   - 1. 7 1 7, \end{array}
$$

$H _ { 0 }$ is clearly rejected at an $\alpha = 0 . 0 5$ significance level. Notice that the approximate p-value of this test is 0.005 because $- t _ { 0 . 0 0 5 } ( 2 2 ) = - 2 . 8 1 9$ . (See Figure 8.2-1.) Notice also that the sample variances do not differ too much; thus, most statisticians would use this two-sample t test.

Assuming independent random samples of sizes $n _ { X }$ and $n _ { Y }$ , let ${ \overline { { x } } } , { \overline { { y } } } ,$ and $s _ { P } ^ { 2 }$ represent the observed unbiased estimates of the respective parameters $\mu _ { X } , \mu _ { Y }$ , and $\sigma _ { X } ^ { 2 } = \sigma _ { Y } ^ { 2 }$ of two normal distributions with a common variance. $$
\overline {{x}} - \overline {{y}} - t _ {\alpha} (n _ {X} + n _ {Y} - 2) s _ {P} \sqrt {1 / n _ {X} + 1 / n _ {Y}}.
$$

A product is packaged by a machine with 24 filler heads numbered 1 to 24, with the odd-numbered heads on one side of the machine and the even on the other side. To perform the test, after the machine has been set up and is running, we shall select one package at random from each filler head and weigh it. The test statistic is that given by Equation 8.2-1 with $n _ { X } = n _ { Y } = 1 2$ . At an $\alpha = 0 . 1 0$ significance level, the critical region is $| t | \geq t _ { 0 . 0 5 } ( 2 2 ) = 1 . 7 1 7$

The box plots in Figure 8.2-3 were constructed with the use of the fivenumber summary for the observations of X (1067, 1072, 1077, 1081.5, and 1084) and the five-number summary for the observations of Y (1064, 1068.25, 1072.5, 1075, and 1082). We would like to give two modifications of tests about two means. First, if we are able to assume that we know the variances of X and Y, then the appropriate test statistic to use for testing H<sub>0</sub>: $\mu _ { X } = \mu _ { Y }$ is 

$$
Z = \frac {\overline {{X}} - \overline {{Y}}}{\sqrt {\frac {\sigma_ {X} ^ {2}}{n _ {X}} + \frac {\sigma_ {Y} ^ {2}}{n _ {Y}}}},\tag{8.2-3}
$$

which has a standard normal distribution when the null hypothesis is true and, of course, when the populations are normally distributed. Second, if the variances are unknown and the sample sizes are large, replace $\sigma _ { X } ^ { 2 }$ with $S _ { X } ^ { 2 }$ and $\sigma _ { Y } ^ { 2 }$ with $S _ { Y } ^ { 2 }$ in Equation 8.2-3. The resulting statistic will have an approximate $N ( 0 , 1 )$ distribution. 

The target thickness for Fruit Flavored Gum and for Fruit Flavored Bubble Gum is 6.7 hundredths of an inch. Let the independent random variables X and Y equal the respective thicknesses of these gums in hundredths of an inch, and assume that their distributions are $N ( \mu _ { X } , \sigma _ { X } ^ { 2 } )$ and $N ( \mu _ { Y } , \sigma _ { Y } ^ { 2 } )$ , respectively. Because bubble gum has more elasticity than regular gum, it may be harder to roll it out to the correct thickness. Thus, we shall test the null hypothesis $H _ { 0 } \colon \mu _ { X } = \mu _ { Y }$ against the alternative hypothesis $H _ { 1 } \colon \mu _ { X } < \mu _ { Y }$ , using samples of sizes $n _ { X } = 5 0$ and $n _ { Y } = 4 0$ 

Because the variances are unknown and the sample sizes are large, the test statistic that is used is 

$$
Z = \frac {\overline {{X}} - \overline {{Y}}}{\sqrt {\frac {S _ {X} ^ {2}}{5 0} + \frac {S _ {Y} ^ {2}}{4 0}}}.
$$

This graphical display also confirms our conclusion. 

REMARK For statistical tests to perform as designed, the assumptions on which they are based must be satisfied reasonably well. As long as the underlying distributions are not highly skewed, the normality assumptions are not too critical, as X and 

Y have approximate normal distributions by the central limit theorem. As distributions become nonnormal and highly skewed, the sample mean and sample variance become more dependent, and that causes problems in using the Student’s t as an approximating distribution for T. In these cases, some of the nonparametric methods described later will usually perform better. (See Section 8.5.) 

When the distributions are close to normal but the variances seem to differ by a great deal, the t statistic should again be avoided, particularly if the sample sizes are also different. In that case, use Z or the modification produced by substituting the sample variances for the distribution variances. In the latter situation, if $n _ { X }$ and $n _ { Y }$ are large enough, there is no problem. With small $n _ { X }$ and $n _ { Y }$ , most statisticians would use Welch’s suggestion (or other modifications of it); that is, they would use an approximating Student’s t distribution with r degrees of freedom where r is given by Equation 7.2-1. Alternatively, nonparametric methods described in Section 8.5 could be used. 

## Exercises

In some of the exercises that follow, we must make assumptions such as the existence of normal distributions with equal variances. 

8.2-1. The botanist in Example 8.2-2 is really interested in testing for synergistic interaction. That is, given the two hormones gibberellin (GA ) and indoleacetic acid (IAA), let $X _ { 1 }$ and ${ \breve { X } } _ { 2 }$ equal the growth responses (in mm) of dwarf pea stem segments to $\mathrm { G A } _ { 3 }$ and IAA, respectively and separately. Also, let $X = X _ { 1 } + X _ { 2 }$ and let Y equal the growth response when both hormones are present. Assuming that X is $N ( \mu _ { X } , \sigma ^ { 2 } )$ and Y is $N ( \mu _ { Y } , \sigma ^ { 2 } )$ , the botanist is interested in testing the hypothesis H<sub>0</sub>: $\mu _ { X } ~ = ~ \mu _ { Y }$ against the alternative hypothesis of synergistic interaction $H _ { 1 } \colon \mu _ { X } < \mu _ { Y }$ 

(a) Using $n _ { X } = n _ { Y } = 1 0$ observations of X and Y, define the test statistic and the critical region. Sketch a figure of the t pdf and show the critical region on your figure. Let α = 0.05. 

(b) Given $n _ { X } = 1 0$ observations of X, namely, 

and $n _ { Y } = 1 0$ observations of Y, namely, 

calculate the value of the test statistic and state your conclusion. Locate the test statistic on your figure.

## 8.3 TESTS FOR VARIANCES

Sometimes the testing problem of interest involves hypotheses about a variance (or equivalently, a standard deviation) of a normal distribution, or about the variances (or standard deviations) of two normal distributions. In this section we describe procedures for testing such hypotheses. 

To motivate the need for such tests, we note that in the manufacturing processes of many products, having small variability among the items produced is very important. Consider a case in which pills are produced for treating a certain medical condition. It is critical that every pill have close to the recommended amount of the active ingredient because too little could render the pill ineffective and too much could be toxic. Suppose that a well-established manufacturing process produces pills for which the standard deviation of the amount of active ingredient is 0.6 micrograms. Suppose further that a pharmaceutical company has developed a new process for producing the pills that it thinks may reduce this standard deviation. Accordingly, the company wants to test the null hypothesis $H _ { 0 } \colon \sigma \ = \ 0 . 6$ against the alternative hypothesis $H _ { 1 } \colon \sigma < 0 . 6 . \ : \mathrm { A }$ random sample of n pills is taken from the production line using the new process, and a test of $H _ { 0 }$ against $H _ { 1 }$ will be based on the sample standard deviation $S$ of the amount of active ingredient measured in these $n$ pills. More specifically, it seems reasonable to reject the null hypothesis if and only if the sample standard deviation is sufficiently less than 0.6. 

But how, exactly, should we measure the discrepancy between S and 0.6? By analogy with how we measured the discrepancy between $\overrightharpoon { X }$ and the mean $\mu$ of a normal distribution when testing hypotheses about $\mu ,$ we might initially consider using the scaled difference $( S - 0 . \bar { 6 } ) / \sqrt { \mathrm { V a r } ( S ) }$ . However, there are several difficulties with this measure, not the least of which is that S is inherently nonnegative, which leads to an asymmetry: the numerator of the scaled difference is bounded by $- 0 . 6$ on the left but is unbounded on the right. It turns out that a better and more convenient discrepancy measure is the ratio $S / 0 . 6$ , and even more convenient is the squared and scaled ratio, 

$$
\chi^ {2} = \frac {(n - 1) S ^ {2}}{0 . 6 ^ {2}}.
$$

The reason this statistic is labeled as $\chi ^ { 2 }$ is that it has a chi-square distribution with $n - 1$ degrees of freedom when $H _ { 0 }$ is true, provided that the sampled population is normally distributed (Theorem 5.5-2). Because the expectation of a chi-square distribution with $n - 1$ degrees of freedom is $n - 1$ , we see that the further that $\textstyle { \dot { \chi } } ^ { 2 }$ is from $n - 1$ , the greater the discrepancy between the observed value of S and the value of the population standard deviation claimed by the null hypothesis. Accordingly, we will use $\chi ^ { 2 }$ as our test statistic and will reject $H _ { 0 } \colon \sigma = 0 . 6$ in favor of $H _ { 1 } \colon \sigma \ < \ 0 . 6$ if and only if 

$$
\chi^ {2} <   \chi_ {1 - \alpha} ^ {2} (n - 1),
$$

where α is the level of significance of the test. 

Suppose that, in the preceding discussion, $n = 2 3 , \alpha = 0 . 0 5$ , and the sample standard deviation was $s = 0 . 4 2 ;$ equivalently, the sample variance was $s ^ { 2 } = 0 . 4 \hat { 2 } ^ { 2 } = 0 . 1 7 6 4$ To test $H _ { 0 } \colon \sigma = 0 . 6$ against $H _ { 1 } \colon \sigma < 0 . 6$ , we compute the test statistic 

$$
\chi^ {2} = \frac {(n - 1) s ^ {2}}{0 . 6 ^ {2}} = \frac {(2 2) (0 . 1 7 6 4)}{0 . 3 6} = 1 0. 7 8.
$$

Comparing this to $\chi _ { 0 . 9 5 } ^ { 2 } ( 2 2 ) = 1 2 . 3 4$ , we reject $H _ { 0 }$ . In other words, it can be concluded, at the 0.05 level of significance, that the new production process reduces the variability in the amount of active ingredient in the pills. 

Table 8.3-1 summarizes tests of hypotheses about a single standard deviation (or variance) for both one-sided alternative hypotheses and the two-sided alternative. In the table, $\sigma _ { 0 } ^ { 2 }$ represents the value of $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ claimed by the null hypothesis. Note that for these tests to be used, it is important that the population being sampled is normal or very nearly so; the performance of the test can be poor if the population is nonnormal, even if the sample size is large, so the test should not be used in that case. 

We can also find $p \mathrm { - }$ values for tests about a variance. In Example 8.3-1, the p-value is 

$$
p \text {-value} = P (W \leq 1 0. 7 8),
$$

<table><tr><td colspan="3">Table 8.3-1 Tests About the Variance</td></tr><tr><td><eq>H_0</eq></td><td><eq>H_1</eq></td><td>Critical Region</td></tr><tr><td><eq>\sigma^2 = \sigma_0^2</eq></td><td><eq>\sigma^2 &gt; \sigma_0^2</eq></td><td><eq>s^2 \geq \frac{\sigma_0^2 \chi_\alpha^2(n-1)}{n-1} \text{ or } \chi^2 \geq \chi_\alpha^2(n-1)</eq></td></tr><tr><td><eq>\sigma^2 = \sigma_0^2</eq></td><td><eq>\sigma^2 &lt; \sigma_0^2</eq></td><td><eq>s^2 \leq \frac{\sigma_0^2 \chi_{1-\alpha}^2(n-1)}{n-1} \text{ or } \chi^2 \leq \chi_{1-\alpha}^2(n-1)</eq></td></tr><tr><td><eq>\sigma^2 = \sigma_0^2</eq></td><td><eq>\sigma^2 \neq \sigma_0^2</eq></td><td><eq>s^2 \leq \frac{\sigma_0^2 \chi_{1-\alpha/2}^2(n-1)}{n-1} \text{ or } s^2 \geq \frac{\sigma_0^2 \chi_\alpha^2(n-1)}{n-1}</eq>or <eq>\chi^2 \leq \chi_{1-\alpha/2}^2(n-1) \text{ or } \chi^2 \geq \chi_{\alpha/2}^2(n-1)</eq></td></tr></table>

where W has a chi-square distribution with 22 degrees of freedom. From Table IV in Appendix B, we see that 

$$
P (W \leq 1 0. 9 8) = 0. 0 2 5 \quad \text { and } \quad P (W \leq 9. 5 4 2) = 0. 0 1.
$$

Thus, 

$$
0. 0 1 <   p \text {-value} <   0. 0 2 5,
$$

and the null hypothesis would be rejected at the 0.025 level but not at the 0.01 level of significance. To find the p-value for a two-sided alternative, we double the tail probability beyond the computed chi-square test statistic if the sample variance is larger than $\sigma _ { 0 } ^ { 2 }$ or we double the tail probability below the chi-square test statistic if the sample variance is less than $\sigma _ { 0 } ^ { 2 }$ . If, in Example 8.3-1, the alternative hypothesis had been two-sided, thep-value would have been $2 P ( W \leq 1 0 . 7 8 )$ , which lies between 0.02 and 0.05. 

Suppose that instead of testing hypotheses about the variance $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ of a normal distribution, we wish to have a confidence interval for it. Suppose further that we have taken a random sample from this distribution, for which the observed sample variance is $s ^ { 2 }$ . Because $( n - 1 ) S ^ { 2 } / \sigma ^ { 2 }$ has a chi-square distribution with $n - 1$ degrees of freedom, we have, for any $\alpha \in ( 0 , 1 )$ , 

$$
P \left(\chi_ {1 - \alpha / 2} ^ {2} (n - 1) \leq \frac {(n - 1) S ^ {2}}{\sigma^ {2}} \leq \chi_ {\alpha / 2} ^ {2} (n - 1)\right) = 1 - \alpha .
$$

The inequalities inside the parentheses can be manipulated algebraically by dividing through by $( n - 1 ) S ^ { 2 }$ , reciprocating the results, and appropriately changing the direction of the inequalities to yield the equivalent probability statement 

$$
P \left(\frac {(n - 1) S ^ {2}}{\chi_ {\alpha / 2} ^ {2} (n - 1)} \leq \sigma^ {2} \leq \frac {(n - 1) S ^ {2}}{\chi_ {1 - \alpha / 2} ^ {2} (n - 1)}\right) = 1 - \alpha .
$$

Thus, a $1 0 0 ( 1 { - } \alpha ) \%$ two-sided confidence interval for $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ , assuming that the randomly sampled population is normal, is given by 

$$
\left[ \frac {(n - 1) s ^ {2}}{\chi_ {\alpha / 2} ^ {2} (n - 1)}, \frac {(n - 1) s ^ {2}}{\chi_ {1 - \alpha / 2} ^ {2} (n - 1)} \right].
$$

Observe that, in contrast to the two-sided confidence intervals for means and proportions introduced in Chapter $^ 7 ,$ the endpoints of the interval are not obtained by adding or subtracting the same quantity to the point estimate $s ^ { 2 }$ . Thus, $s ^ { 2 }$ generally is not located at the midpoint of the interval. Note also that we can obtain a $1 0 0 ( 1 { - } \alpha ) \%$ confidence interval for σ merely by taking positive square roots of the endpoints. 

To illustrate, let us obtain a $9 5 \%$ two-sided confidence interval for the variance of the amount of active ingredient in the pills described earlier in this section, using the results from a sample of size $n = 2 3$ given in Example 8.3-1. The desired interval is 

$$
\left[ \frac {(2 2) (0 . 1 7 6 4)}{\chi_ {0 . 0 5} ^ {2} (2 2)}, \frac {(2 2) (0 . 1 7 6 4)}{\chi_ {0 . 9 5} ^ {2} (2 2)} \right] = \left[ \frac {(2 2) (0 . 1 7 6 4)}{3 3 . 9 2}, \frac {(2 2) (0 . 1 7 6 4)}{1 2 . 3 4} \right] = [ 0. 1 1 4 4, 0. 3 1 4 5 ].
$$

The other test about variances we present here is a test for the equality of variances from two independently sampled normal populations. Let the independent random variables $X$ and Y have respective distributions that are $N ( \mu _ { X } , \hat { \sigma } _ { X } ^ { 2 } )$ and $N ( \mu _ { Y } , \sigma _ { Y } ^ { 2 } )$ . To test the null hypothesis $H _ { 0 } \colon \sigma _ { X } ^ { 2 } / \sigma _ { Y } ^ { 2 } = 1$ (or, equivalently, $\sigma _ { X } ^ { 2 } = \sigma _ { Y } ^ { 2 } )$ take random samples of $n _ { X }$ observations of $X$ and $n _ { Y }$ observations of Y. Now $( n _ { X } - 1 ) S _ { X } ^ { 2 } / \sigma _ { X } ^ { 2 }$ and $\hat { ( } n _ { Y } - 1 ) S _ { Y } ^ { 2 } / \sigma _ { Y } ^ { 2 }$ have independent chi-square distributions $\chi ^ { 2 } ( n _ { X } - 1 )$ and $\chi ^ { 2 } ( n _ { Y } - 1 )$ , respectively. Thus, when $H _ { 0 }$ is true, 

$$
F = \frac {\frac {(n _ {X} - 1) S _ {X} ^ {2}}{\sigma_ {X} ^ {2} (n _ {X} - 1)}}{\frac {(n _ {Y} - 1) S _ {Y} ^ {2}}{\sigma_ {Y} ^ {2} (n _ {Y} - 1)}} = \frac {S _ {X} ^ {2}}{S _ {Y} ^ {2}}
$$

has an F distribution with $r _ { 1 } = n _ { X } - 1$ and $r _ { 2 } = n _ { Y } - 1$ degrees of freedom. This F statistic is our test statistic. When $H _ { 0 }$ is true, we would expect the observed value of F to be close to 1. 

With normal distributions, three possible alternative hypotheses, along with critical regions of size α, are summarized in Table 8.3-2. Recall that $1 / F$ , the reciprocal of $F ,$ has an F distribution with $n _ { Y } - 1$ and $n _ { X } - 1$ degrees of freedom so all cases may be written in terms of right-tail critical regions and the critical values can be selected easily from Table VII in Appendix B. 


Table 8.3-2 Tests of Hypotheses of the Equality of Variances

In case it is desired to have a confidence interval for the ratio of two variances, consider the following. Using the fact, noted earlier in this section, that the distribution of 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \frac {(n _ {Y} - 1) S _ {Y} ^ {2}}{\sigma_ {Y} ^ {2} (n _ {Y} - 1)} \\ \frac {(n _ {X} - 1) S _ {X} ^ {2}}{\sigma_ {X} ^ {2} (n _ {X} - 1)} \end{array}
$$

is $F ( n _ { Y } - 1 , n _ { X } - 1 )$ , we have 

$$
\begin{array}{c} 1 - \alpha = P \bigg [ F _ {1 - \alpha / 2} (n _ {Y} - 1, n _ {X} - 1) \leq \frac {S _ {Y} ^ {2} / \sigma_ {Y} ^ {2}}{S _ {X} ^ {2} / \sigma_ {X} ^ {2}} \leq F _ {\alpha / 2} (n _ {Y} - 1, n _ {X} - 1) \bigg ] \\ = P \bigg [ F _ {1 - \alpha / 2} (n _ {Y} - 1, n _ {X} - 1) (S _ {X} ^ {2} / S _ {Y} ^ {2}) \leq \frac {\sigma_ {X} ^ {2}}{\sigma_ {Y} ^ {2}} \leq F _ {\alpha / 2} (n _ {Y} - 1, n _ {X} - 1) (S _ {X} ^ {2} / S _ {Y} ^ {2}) \bigg ]. \end{array}
$$

Thus 

$$
\left[ F _ {1 - \alpha / 2} (n _ {Y} - 1, n _ {X} - 1) (S _ {X} ^ {2} / S _ {Y} ^ {2}), F _ {\alpha / 2} (n _ {Y} - 1, n _ {X} - 1) (S _ {X} ^ {2} / S _ {Y} ^ {2}) \right],
$$

or equivalently 

$$
\left[ \frac {S _ {X} ^ {2} / S _ {Y} ^ {2}}{F _ {\alpha / 2} (n _ {X} - 1 , n _ {Y} - 1)}, F _ {\alpha / 2} (n _ {Y} - 1, n _ {X} - 1) (S _ {X} ^ {2} / S _ {Y} ^ {2}) \right],
$$

is a $1 0 0 ( 1 - \alpha ) \%$ confidence interval for $\sigma _ { X } ^ { 2 } / \sigma _ { Y } ^ { 2 }$

## 8.4 TESTS ABOUT PROPORTIONS

Suppose a manufacturer of a certain printed circuit observes that approximately a proportion $p = 0 . 0 6$ of the circuits fail. An engineer and statistician working together suggest some changes that might improve the design of the product. To test this new procedure, it was agreed that $n = 2 0 0$ circuits would be produced by the proposed method and then checked. Let Y equal the number of these 200 circuits that fail. Clearly, if the number of failures, Y, is such that $Y / 2 0 0$ is about equal to 0.06, then it seems that the new procedure has not resulted in an improvement. Also, on the one hand, if Y is small so that Y/200 is about 0.02 or 0.03, we might believe that the new method is better than the old. On the other hand, if Y/200 is 0.09 or 0.10, the proposed method has perhaps caused a greater proportion of failures. 

What we need to establish is a formal rule that tells us when to accept the new procedure as an improvement. In addition, we must know the consequences of this rule. As an example of such a rule, we could declare the new procedure as an improvement if $Y \ \le \ 7$ or equivalently $Y / n ~ \le ~ 0 . 0 3 5$ . We do note, however, that we could observe seven or fewer failures in $n = 2 0 0$ trials even if the probability of failure is still $p = 0 . 0 6$ . That is, we could erroneously declare the new method an improvement when, in fact, it was not. This would be an instance of a Type I error. In contrast, the new procedure might actually improve the product so that p is much smaller, say, $p = 0 . 0 3$ , and yet we could observe $y = 9$ failures, so that $y / 2 0 0 = 0 . 0 4 5$ . Thus, we could, again erroneously, not declare the new method as resulting in an improvement when, in fact, it had. This would be a Type II error. We must study the probabilities of these two types of errors to understand fully the consequences of our rule. 

Let us begin by modeling the situation. If we believe that these trials, conducted under the new procedure, are independent, and that each trial has the same probability p of failure, then Y is binomial $b ( 2 0 0 , p )$ . We wish to make a statistical inference about p using the unbiased estimator $\widehat { p } \ = \ Y / 2 0 0 .$ . Of course, we could construct a one-sided confidence interval—say, one that has 95% confidence of providing an upper bound for p—and obtain 

$$
\left[ 0, \widehat {p} + 1. 6 4 5 \sqrt {\frac {\widehat {p} (1 - \widehat {p})}{2 0 0}} \right].
$$

This inference is appropriate and many statisticians simply make it. If the limits of this confidence interval contain 0.06, they would not say that the new procedure is necessarily better, at least until more data are taken. If, however, the upper limit of the confidence interval is less than 0.06, then those same statisticians would feel 95% confident that the true $p$ is now less than 0.06. Hence, they would support the conclusion that the new procedure has improved the manufacturing of the printed circuits in question. 

This use of a confidence interval for $_ p$ is related to hypothesis testing for $p ,$ which we now describe in detail. Here, in our illustration, we are testing whether the probability of failure has or has not decreased from 0.06 when the new manufacturing procedure is used. The null hypothesis is $H _ { 0 } ; p = 0 . 0 6$ and the alternative hypothesis is $H _ { 1 } \colon p \ < \ 0 . 0 6$ . Because, in our illustration, we make a Type I error if $Y \le 7$ when, in fact, $p = 0 . 0 6$ , we can calculate the probability of this error. We denote that probability by $\alpha$ and call it the significance level of the test. Under our assumptions, it is 

$$
\alpha = P (Y \leq 7; p = 0. 0 6) = \sum_ {y = 0} ^ {7} \binom {2 0 0} {y} (0. 0 6) ^ {y} (0. 9 4) ^ {2 0 0 - y}.
$$

Because n is rather large and $p$ is small, these binomial probabilities can be approximated very well by Poisson probabilities with $\lambda = 2 0 0 ( 0 . 0 6 ) = 1 2$ . That is, from the Poisson table, the probability of a Type I error is 

$$
\alpha \approx \sum_ {y = 0} ^ {7} \frac {1 2 ^ {y} e ^ {- 1 2}}{y !} = 0. 0 9 0.
$$

Thus, the approximate significance level of this test is $\alpha = 0 . 0 9 0 .$ (Using the binomial distribution, we find that the exact value of α is 0.0829, which you can easily verify with Minitab.) 

This value of $\alpha$ is reasonably small. However, what about the probability of a Type II error in case $p$ has been improved to, say, 0.03? This error occurs if $\dot { Y } > 7$ when, in fact, $p = 0 . 0 3 ;$ hence, its probability, denoted by $\beta ,$ is 

$$
\beta = P (Y > 7; p = 0. 0 3) = \sum_ {y = 8} ^ {2 0 0} \binom {2 0 0} {y} (0. 0 3) ^ {y} (0. 9 7) ^ {2 0 0 - y}.
$$

Again, we use the Poisson approximation, here with $\lambda = 2 0 0 ( 0 . 0 3 ) = 6 .$ , to obtain 

$$
\beta \approx 1 - \sum_ {y = 0} ^ {7} \frac {6 ^ {y} e ^ {- 6}}{y !} = 1 - 0. 7 4 4 = 0. 2 5 6.
$$

(The binomial distribution tells us that the exact probability is 0.2539, so the approximation is very good.) The engineer and the statistician who created the new procedure probably are not too pleased with this answer. That is, they might note that if their new procedure of manufacturing circuits has actually decreased the probability of failure to 0.03 from 0.06 (a big improvement), there is still a good chance, 0.256, that $H _ { 0 } ; p = 0 . 0 6$ is accepted and their improvement rejected. In Section 8.6, more will be said about modifying tests so that satisfactory values of the probabilities of the two types of errors, namely, α and $\beta ,$ can be obtained; however, to decrease both of them, we need larger sample sizes. 

Without worrying more about the probability of the Type II error here, we present a frequently used procedure for testing $H _ { 0 } { : } p = p _ { 0 }$ , where $p _ { 0 }$ is some specified probability of success. This test is based upon the fact that the number of successes Y in n independent Bernoulli trials is such that $Y / n$ has an approximate normal distribution $\bar { N [ p _ { 0 } , p _ { 0 } ( 1 - p _ { 0 } ) / n ] }$ , provided that $H _ { 0 } \colon p = p _ { 0 }$ is true and n is large. Suppose the alternative hypothesis is $H _ { 1 } \colon p \ > \ p _ { 0 } ;$ that is, it is hypothesized that something has been done to increase the probability of success. Consider the test of $H _ { 0 } { : } p = p _ { 0 }$ against $H _ { 1 } { : } p > p _ { 0 }$ that rejects $H _ { 0 }$ if and only if 

$$
Z = \frac {Y / n - p _ {0}}{\sqrt {p _ {0} (1 - p _ {0}) / n}} \geq z _ {\alpha}.
$$

That is, if $Y / n$ exceeds $p _ { 0 }$ by $z _ { \alpha }$ standard deviations of $Y / n ,$ we reject $H _ { 0 }$ and conclude that $p > p _ { 0 }$ . Because, under $H _ { 0 } , Z$ is approximately $N ( 0 , 1 )$ , the approximate probability of this occurring when $H _ { 0 } { : } p = p _ { 0 }$ is true is α. So the significance level of this test is approximately α. 

If the alternative is $H _ { 1 } { : } p < p _ { 0 }$ instead of $H _ { 1 } { : } p > p _ { 0 }$ , then the appropriate α-level test is given by $Z \le - z _ { \alpha }$ . Hence, if $Y / n$ is smaller than $p _ { 0 }$ by $z _ { \alpha }$ standard deviations of $Y / n ,$ , we can conclude that $p < p _ { 0 }$ 

It was claimed that many commercially manufactured dice are not fair because the “spots” are really indentations, so that, for example, the 6-side is lighter than the 1- side. Let p equal the probability of rolling a six with one of these dice. To test $H _ { 0 } \colon$ $p = 1 / 6$ against the alternative hypothesis $H _ { 1 } \colon p \ > \ 1 / 6$ , several such dice will be rolled to yield a total of $n = 8 0 0 0$ observations. Let Y equal the number of times that six resulted in the 8000 trials. The test statistic is 

$$
Z = \frac {Y / n - 1 / 6}{\sqrt {(1 / 6) (5 / 6) / n}} = \frac {Y / 8 0 0 0 - 1 / 6}{\sqrt {(1 / 6) (5 / 6) / 8 0 0 0}}.
$$

If we use a significance level of $\alpha = 0 . 0 5$ , the critical region is 

$$
z \geq z _ {0. 0 5} = 1. 6 4 5.
$$

The results of the experiment yielded $y = 1 3 8 9 .$ , so the calculated value of the test statistic is 

$$
z = \frac {1 3 8 9 / 8 0 0 0 - 1 / 6}{\sqrt {(1 / 6) (5 / 6) / 8 0 0 0}} = 1. 6 7 0.
$$

Because 

$$
z = 1. 6 7 0 > 1. 6 4 5,
$$

the null hypothesis is rejected, and the experimental results indicate that these dice favor a six more than a fair die would. (You could perform your own experiment to check out other dice.) 

There are times when a two-sided alternative is appropriate; that is, a test of $H _ { 0 } \colon$ $p = p _ { 0 }$ against $H _ { 1 } { : } p \neq p _ { 0 }$ . For example, suppose that the pass rate in the usual beginning statistics course is $p _ { 0 }$ . There has been an intervention (say, some new teaching method) and it is not known whether the pass rate will increase, decrease, or stay about the same. Thus, we test the null (no-change) hypothesis $H _ { 0 } { : } p = p _ { 0 }$ against the 

<!-- === Source: MinerU_markdown_Robert_V._Hogg,_Elliot_A._Tanis,_Dale_L._Zimmerman_-_Probability_and_Statistical_Inference-Pearson_(2021)_401_2122706224590991361.md (Page 401) === -->

<table><tr><td colspan="3">Table 8.4-1 Tests of hypotheses for one proportion</td></tr><tr><td><eq>H_0</eq></td><td><eq>H_1</eq></td><td>Critical Region</td></tr><tr><td><eq>p = p_0</eq></td><td><eq>p &gt; p_0</eq></td><td><eq>z = \frac{y/n - p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1 - p_0)/n}} \geq z_\alpha</eq></td></tr><tr><td><eq>p = p_0</eq></td><td><eq>p &lt; p_0</eq></td><td><eq>z = \frac{y/n - p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1 - p_0)/n}} \leq -z_\alpha</eq></td></tr><tr><td><eq>p = p_0</eq></td><td><eq>p \neq p_0</eq></td><td><eq>|z| = \frac{|y/n - p_0|}{\sqrt{p_0(1 - p_0)/n}} \geq z_{\alpha/2}</eq></td></tr></table>

two-sided alternative $H _ { 1 } ; p \neq p _ { 0 } . \mathbf { A }$ test with the approximate significance level α for doing this is to reject H : $p = p _ { 0 }$ if 

$$
| Z | = \frac {| Y / n - p _ {0} |}{\sqrt {p _ {0} (1 - p _ {0}) / n}} \geq z _ {\alpha / 2},
$$

because, under $H _ { 0 } , P ( | Z | \geq z _ { \alpha / 2 } ) \approx \alpha$ . These tests of approximate significance level α are summarized in Table 8.4-1. 

Recall that the p-value associated with a test is the probability, under the null hypothesis $H _ { 0 }$ , that the test statistic (a random variable) is equal to or more extreme than the observed value (a constant) of the test statistic in the direction(s) of the alternative hypothesis. Rather than select the critical region ahead of time, the $p \mathrm { - }$ value of a test can be reported and the reader then makes a decision. In Example 8.4- 1, the value of the test statistic was $z = 1 . 6 7$ . Because the alternative hypothesis was $H _ { 1 } ; p > 1 / 6$ , the p-value is 

$$
P (Z \geq 1. 6 7) = 0. 0 4 7 5.
$$

Note that this p-value is less than $\alpha = 0 . 0 5$ , which would lead to the rejection of $H _ { 0 }$ at an $\alpha = 0 . 0 5$ significance level. If the alternative hypothesis were two-sided, $H _ { 1 } ;$ $p \neq 1 / 6 ,$ , then the p-value would be $P ( | Z | \geq 1 . 6 7 ) = 0 . 0 9 5$ and would not lead to the rejection of $H _ { 0 }$ at $\alpha = 0 . 0 5$ 

Often there is interest in tests about $p _ { 1 }$ and $p _ { 2 }$ , the probabilities of success for two distributions or the proportions of two populations having a certain characteristic. For example, if $p _ { 1 }$ and $p _ { 2 }$ denote the respective proportions of homeowners and renters who vote in favor of a proposal to reduce property taxes, a politician might be interested in testing H : $p _ { 1 } = p _ { 2 }$ against the one-sided alternative hypothesis $H _ { 1 }$ : $p _ { 1 } > p _ { 2 }$ 

Let $Y _ { 1 }$ and $Y _ { 2 }$ represent, respectively, the numbers of observed successes in $n _ { 1 }$ and $n _ { 2 }$ independent Bernoulli trials with probabilities of success $p _ { 1 }$ and $p _ { 2 }$ . Recall that the distribution of ${ \widehat { p } } _ { 1 } = Y _ { 1 / n _ { 1 } }$ is approximately $N [ p _ { 1 } , p _ { 1 } ( 1 - p _ { 1 } ) / n _ { 1 } ]$ and the distribution of $\widehat { p } _ { 2 } = Y _ { 2 } / n _ { 2 }$ is approximately $N [ p _ { 2 } , p _ { 2 } ( 1 - p _ { 2 } ) / n _ { 2 } ]$ . Thus, the distribution of ${ \widehat { p } } _ { 1 } { - } { \widehat { p } } _ { 2 } = Y _ { 1 } / n _ { 1 } { - } Y _ { 2 } / n _ { 2 }$ is approximately $N [ p _ { 1 } - p _ { 2 } , p _ { 1 } ( 1 - p _ { 1 } ) / n _ { 1 } + p _ { 2 } ( 1 - p _ { 2 } ) / n _ { 2 } ]$ It follows that the distribution of 

$$
Z = \frac {Y _ {1} / n _ {1} - Y _ {2} / n _ {2} - (p _ {1} - p _ {2})}{\sqrt {p _ {1} (1 - p _ {1}) / n _ {1} + p _ {2} (1 - p _ {2}) / n _ {2}}}\tag{8.4-1}
$$

is approximately $N ( 0 , 1 )$ . To test H : $p _ { 1 } - p _ { 2 } = 0$ or, equivalently, H<sub>0</sub>: $p _ { 1 } ~ = ~ p _ { 2 }$ let $p \ = \ p _ { 1 } \ = \ p _ { 2 }$ be the common value under $H _ { 0 }$ . We shall estimate $p$ with $\widehat { p } =$ $( Y _ { 1 } + Y _ { 2 } ) / ( n _ { 1 } + n _ { 2 } )$ . Replacing $p _ { 1 }$ and $p _ { 2 }$ in the denominator of Equation 8.4-1 with this estimate, we obtain the test statistic 

<table><tr><td colspan="3">Table 8.4-2 Tests of Hypotheses for two proportions</td></tr><tr><td><eq>H_0</eq></td><td><eq>H_1</eq></td><td>Critical Region</td></tr><tr><td><eq>p_1 = p_2</eq></td><td><eq>p_1 &gt; p_2</eq></td><td><eq>z = \frac{\widehat{p}_1 - \widehat{p}_2}{\sqrt{\widehat{p}(1 - \widehat{p})(1/n_1 + 1/n_2)}} \geq z_\alpha</eq></td></tr><tr><td><eq>p_1 = p_2</eq></td><td><eq>p_1 &lt; p_2</eq></td><td><eq>z = \frac{\widehat{p}_1 - \widehat{p}_2}{\sqrt{\widehat{p}(1 - \widehat{p})(1/n_1 + 1/n_2)}} \leq -z_\alpha</eq></td></tr><tr><td><eq>p_1 = p_2</eq></td><td><eq>p_1 \neq p_2</eq></td><td><eq>|z| = \frac{|\widehat{p}_1 - \widehat{p}_2|}{\sqrt{\widehat{p}(1 - \widehat{p})(1/n_1 + 1/n_2)}} \geq z_{\alpha/2}</eq></td></tr></table>

$$
Z = \frac {\widehat {p} _ {1} - \widehat {p} _ {2} - 0}{\sqrt {\widehat {p} (1 - \widehat {p}) (1 / n _ {1} + 1 / n _ {2})}},
$$

which has an approximate $N ( 0 , 1 )$ distribution when the null hypothesis is true. 

The three possible alternative hypotheses and their critical regions are summarized in Table 8.4-2. 

REMARK In testing both H<sub>0</sub>: $p = p _ { 0 }$ and H : $p _ { 1 } = p _ { 2 }$ , statisticians sometimes use different denominators for z. For tests of single proportions, $\sqrt { p _ { 0 } ( 1 - p _ { 0 } ) / n }$ can be replaced by $\sqrt { ( y / n ) ( 1 - y / n ) / n }$ , and for tests of the equality of two proportions, the following denominator can be used: 

$$
\sqrt {\frac {\widehat {p} _ {1} (1 - \widehat {p} _ {1})}{n _ {1}} + \frac {\widehat {p} _ {2} (1 - \widehat {p} _ {2})}{n _ {2}}}.
$$

We do not have a strong preference one way or the other because the two methods provide about the same numerical result. The substitutions do provide better estimates of the standard deviations of the numerators when the null hypotheses are clearly false. There is some advantage to this result if the null hypothesis is likely to be false. In addition, the substitutions tie together the use of confidence intervals and tests of hypotheses. For example, if the null hypothesis is $H _ { 0 } { : } p = p _ { 0 }$ , it is rejected in favor of the alternative hypothesis $H _ { 1 } { : } p < p _ { 0 }$ if 

$$
z = \frac {\widehat {p} - p _ {0}}{\sqrt {\frac {\widehat {p} (1 - \widehat {p})}{n}}} \leq - z _ {\alpha}.
$$

This formula is equivalent to the statement that 

$$
p _ {0} \notin \left[ 0, \widehat {p} + z _ {\alpha} \sqrt {\frac {\widehat {p} (1 - \widehat {p})}{n}}\right),
$$

where the latter is a one-sided confidence interval providing an upper bound for $p .$ Or if the alternative hypothesis is $H _ { 1 } { : } p \neq p _ { 0 }$ , then $H _ { 0 }$ is rejected if 

$$
\frac {| \widehat {p} - p _ {0} |}{\sqrt {\frac {\widehat {p} (1 - \widehat {p})}{n}}} \geq z _ {\alpha / 2}.
$$

This inequality is equivalent to 

$$
p _ {0} \notin \left(\widehat {p} - z _ {\alpha / 2} \sqrt {\frac {\widehat {p} (1 - \widehat {p})}{n}}, \widehat {p} + z _ {\alpha / 2} \sqrt {\frac {\widehat {p} (1 - \widehat {p})}{n}}\right),
$$

where the latter is a confidence interval for $p .$ . However, using the forms given in Tables 8.4-1 and 8.4-2, we do get better approximations to α-level significance tests. Thus, there are trade-offs, and it is difficult to say that one is better than the other. Fortunately, the numerical answers are about the same. 

In the second situation in which the estimates of $p _ { 1 }$ and $p _ { 2 }$ are the observed ${ \widehat { p _ { 1 } } } = y _ { 1 } / n _ { 1 }$ and ${ \widehat { p _ { 2 } } } = y _ { 2 } / n _ { 2 }$ , we have, with large values of $n _ { 1 }$ and $n _ { 2 }$ , an approximate 95% confidence interval for $p _ { 1 } - p _ { 2 }$ given by 

$$
\frac {y _ {1}}{n _ {1}} - \frac {y _ {2}}{n _ {2}} \pm 1. 9 6 \sqrt {\frac {(y _ {1} / n _ {1}) (1 - y _ {1} / n _ {1})}{n _ {1}} + \frac {(y _ {2} / n _ {2}) (1 - y _ {2} / n _ {2})}{n _ {2}}}.
$$

If $p _ { 1 } - p _ { 2 } = 0$ is not in this interval, we reject H : $p _ { 1 } - p _ { 2 } = 0$ at the $\alpha \ : = \ : 0 . 0 5$ significance level. This is equivalent to saying that we reject $H _ { 0 } ; p _ { 1 } - p _ { 2 } = 0$ if 

$$
\frac {\left| \frac {y _ {1}}{n _ {1}} - \frac {y _ {2}}{n _ {2}} \right|}{\sqrt {\frac {(y _ {1} / n _ {1}) (1 - y _ {1} / n _ {1})}{n _ {1}} + \frac {(y _ {2} / n _ {2}) (1 - y _ {2} / n _ {2})}{n _ {2}}}} \geq 1. 9 6.
$$

In general, if the estimator $\widehat { \theta }$ (often, the maximum likelihood estimator) of θ has an approximate (sometimes exact) normal distribution $N ( \theta , \sigma _ { \widehat { \theta } } ^ { 2 } )$ , then $H _ { 0 } \colon \theta = \theta _ { 0 }$ is rejected in favor of $H _ { 1 } \colon \theta \neq \theta _ { 0 }$ at the approximate (sometimes exact) α significance level if 

$$
\theta_ {0} \notin (\widehat {\theta} - z _ {\alpha / 2} \sigma_ {\widehat {\theta}}, \widehat {\theta} + z _ {\alpha / 2} \sigma_ {\widehat {\theta}})
$$

or, equivalently, 

$$
\frac {| \widehat {\theta} - \theta_ {0} |}{\sigma_ {\widehat {\theta}}} \geq z _ {\alpha / 2}.
$$

Note that $\sigma _ { \widehat { \theta } } ^ { \widehat { } }$ often depends upon some unknown parameter that must be estimated and substituted in $\sigma _ { \widehat { \theta } } ^ { \alpha }$ to obtain $\widehat { \sigma _ { \theta } }$ . Sometimes $\sigma _ { \widehat { \theta } } ^ { \alpha }$ or its estimate is called the standard error of ${ \widehat { \theta } } .$ This was the case in our last illustration when, with $\theta \ : = \ : p _ { 1 } - p _ { 2 }$ and ${ \widehat { \theta } } = { \widehat { p _ { 1 } } } - { \widehat { p _ { 2 } } }$ , we substituted $y _ { 1 } / n _ { 1 }$ for $p _ { 1 }$ and $y _ { 2 } / n _ { 2 }$ for $p _ { 2 }$ in 

$$
\sqrt {\frac {p _ {1} (1 - p _ {1})}{n _ {1}} + \frac {p _ {2} (1 - p _ {2})}{n _ {2}}}
$$

to obtain the standard error of ${ \widehat { p _ { 1 } } } - { \widehat { p _ { 2 } } } = { \widehat { \theta } } .$

Draw four balls at random from the bowl, one at a time and with replacement. Let X equal the number of red balls drawn. 

(a) Define a critical region C for this test in terms of $X .$ 

(b) For the critical region C defined in part (a), find the values of α and $\beta .$

8.4-5. If a newborn baby has a birth weight that is less than 2500 grams (5.5 pounds), we say that the baby has a low birth weight. Let p equal the proportion of babies born in the Sudan who weigh less than 2500 grams. We shall test the null hypothesis $H _ { 0 } { : } p = 0 . 0 7$ against the alternative hypothesis $H _ { 1 } \colon p \ > \ 0 . 0 7$ . In a random sample of n = 209 babies, $y = 2 3$ weighed less than 2500 grams.

As mentioned earlier in the text, at times it is clear that the normal assumptions are not met and that other procedures, sometimes referred to as nonparametric or distribution-free methods, should be considered. For example, suppose some hypothesis, say, $H _ { 0 } \colon m = m _ { 0 }$ , against $H _ { 1 } \colon m \neq m _ { 0 }$ , is made about the unknown median, m, of a continuous-type distribution. From the data, we could construct a $1 0 0 ( 1 - \alpha )$ % 

Because $y = 9$ , the null hypothesis is not rejected. 

confidence interval for m, and if $m _ { 0 }$ is not in that interval, we would reject $H _ { 0 }$ at the α significance level. 

Now let X be a continuous-type random variable and let m denote the median of X. To test the hypothesis $H _ { 0 } \colon m = m _ { 0 }$ against an appropriate alternative hypothesis, we could also use a sign test. That is, if $X _ { 1 } , X _ { 2 } , \ldots , X _ { n }$ denote the observations of a random sample from this distribution, and if we let Y equal the number of negative differences among $X _ { 1 } - m _ { 0 } , X _ { 2 } - m _ { 0 } , \ldots , X _ { n } - m _ { 0 }$ , then Y has the binomial distribution $b ( n , 1 / 2 )$ under $H _ { 0 }$ and is the test statistic for the sign test. If Y is too large or too small, we reject $H _ { 0 } \colon m = m _ { 0 }$ 

Let X denote the length of time in seconds between two calls entering a call center. Let m be the unique median of this continuous-type distribution. We test the null hypothesis $H _ { 0 } \colon m = 6 . 2$ against the alternative hypothesis $H _ { 1 } \colon m \ < \ 6 . 2$ . Table II in Appendix B tells us that if Y is the number of lengths of time between calls in a random sample of size 20 that are less than 6.2, then the critical region $C = \{ y : y \geq$ 14} has a significance level of $\alpha = 0 . 0 5 7 7$ . A random sample of size 20 yielded the following data: 

<table><tr><td>6.8</td><td>5.7</td><td>6.9</td><td>5.3</td><td>4.1</td><td>9.8</td><td>1.7</td><td>7.0</td></tr><tr><td>2.1</td><td>19.0</td><td>18.9</td><td>16.9</td><td>10.4</td><td>44.1</td><td>2.9</td><td>2.4</td></tr><tr><td>4.8</td><td>18.9</td><td>4.8</td><td>7.9</td><td></td><td></td><td></td><td></td></tr></table>

The sign test can also be used to test the hypothesis that two possibly dependent continuous-type random variables X and Y are such that $p = P ( X > Y ) = 1 / 2$ To test the hypothesis $H _ { 0 } \colon p \ = \ 1 / 2$ against an appropriate alternative hypothesis, consider the independent pairs $( X _ { 1 } , Y _ { 1 } ) , ( X _ { 2 } , Y _ { 2 } ) , \ldots , ( X _ { n } , Y _ { n } )$ . Let W denote the number of pairs for which $X _ { k } - Y _ { k } > 0$ . When $H _ { 0 }$ is true, W is $b ( n , 1 / 2 )$ , and the test can be based on the statistic W. For example, say X is the length of the right foot of a person and Y the length of the corresponding left foot. Thus, there is a natural pairing, and here $H _ { 0 } ; p = P ( X > Y ) = 1 / 2$ suggests that either foot of a particular individual is equally likely to be longer. 

One major objection to the sign test is that it does not take into account the magnitude of the differences $X _ { 1 } - m _ { 0 } , \ldots , X _ { n } - m _ { 0 }$ . We now discuss a test, known as Wilcoxon’s signed rank test, that does take into account the magnitude of the differences $| X _ { k } - m _ { 0 } | , k = 1 , 2 , \ldots , n$ . However, in addition to assuming that the random variable X is of the continuous type, we must also assume that the pdf of X is symmetric about the median in order to find the distribution of this new statistic. Because of the continuity assumption, we assume, in the discussion that follows, that no two observations are equal and that no observation is equal to the median. 

We are interested in testing the hypothesis $H _ { 0 } ; m = m _ { 0 }$ , where $m _ { 0 }$ is some given constant. With our random sample $X _ { 1 } , X _ { 2 } , \ldots , X _ { n }$ , we rank the absolute values $| X _ { 1 } -$ $m _ { 0 } | , | X _ { 2 } - m _ { 0 } | , \ldots , | X _ { n } - m _ { 0 } |$ in ascending order according to magnitude. That is, for $k = 1 , 2 , \ldots , n .$ , we let $R _ { k }$ denote the rank of $| X _ { k } - m _ { 0 } |$ among $| X _ { 1 } - m _ { 0 } | , | X _ { 2 } -$ $m _ { 0 } | , \ldots , | X _ { n } - m _ { 0 } |$ . Note that $R _ { 1 } , R _ { 2 } , \ldots , R _ { n }$ is a permutation of the first n positive integers, $1 , 2 , \ldots , n$ . Now, with each $R _ { k }$ , we associate the sign of the difference $X _ { k } -$ $m _ { 0 } ;$ that is, if $X _ { k } - m _ { 0 } > 0$ , we use $R _ { k }$ , but if $X _ { k } - m _ { 0 } < 0$ , we use $- R _ { k }$ . The Wilcoxon signed rank statistic W is the sum of these n signed ranks. 

Suppose the lengths of n = 10 sunfish are 

$$
x _ {i}: \begin{array}{l l l l l l l l l l l} 5. 0 & 3. 9 & 5. 2 & 5. 5 & 2. 8 & 6. 1 & 6. 4 & 2. 6 & 1. 7 & 4. 3 \end{array}
$$

We shall test $H _ { 0 } \colon m = 3 . 7$ against the alternative hypothesis $H _ { 1 } \colon m \ > \ 3 . 7$ Thus, we have 

<table><tr><td><eq>x_{k}-m_{0}</eq>:</td><td>1.3,</td><td>0.2,</td><td>1.5,</td><td>1.8,</td><td>-0.9,</td><td>2.4,</td><td>2.7,</td><td>-1.1,</td><td>-2.0,</td><td>0.6</td></tr><tr><td><eq>|x_{k}-m_{0}|</eq>:</td><td>1.3,</td><td>0.2,</td><td>1.5,</td><td>1.8,</td><td>0.9,</td><td>2.4,</td><td>2.7,</td><td>1.1,</td><td>2.0,</td><td>0.6</td></tr><tr><td>Ranks:</td><td>5,</td><td>1,</td><td>6,</td><td>7,</td><td>3,</td><td>9,</td><td>10,</td><td>4,</td><td>8,</td><td>2</td></tr><tr><td>Signed Ranks:</td><td>5,</td><td>1,</td><td>6,</td><td>7,</td><td>-3,</td><td>9,</td><td>10,</td><td>-4,</td><td>-8,</td><td>2</td></tr></table>

Therefore, the Wilcoxon signed rank statistic is equal to 

$$
W = 5 + 1 + 6 + 7 - 3 + 9 + 1 0 - 4 - 8 + 2 = 2 5.
$$

Incidentally, the positive answer seems reasonable because the number of the ten lengths that are less than 3.7 is three, which is the statistic used in the sign test. 

If the hypothesis $H _ { 0 } \colon m = m _ { 0 }$ is true, about one half the differences would be negative and thus about one half the signs would be negative. Hence, it seems that the hypothesis $H _ { 0 } ; m = m _ { 0 }$ is supported if the observed value of W is close to zero. If the alternative hypothesis is $H _ { 1 } \colon m > m _ { 0 }$ , we would reject $H _ { 0 }$ if the observed $W = w$ is too large because, in this case, the larger deviations $| X _ { k } - m _ { 0 } |$ would usually be associated with observations for which $x _ { k } - m _ { 0 } > 0$ . That is, the critical region would be of the form $\{ w : ~ w \geq c _ { 1 } \}$ . If the alternative hypothesis is $H _ { 1 } \colon m < m _ { 0 } .$ , the critical region would be of the form $\{ w : \ w \leq c _ { 2 } \}$ . Of course, the critical region would be of the form {w : $w \leq c _ { 3 } \ \mathrm { o r } \ w \geq c _ { 4 } \}$ for a two-sided alternative hypothesis $H _ { 1 } \colon m \neq m _ { 0 }$ In order to find the values of $c _ { 1 } , c _ { 2 } , c _ { 3 }$ , and $c _ { 4 }$ that yield desired significance levels, it is necessary to determine the distribution of W under $H _ { 0 }$ . Accordingly, we consider certain characteristics of this distribution. 

When $H _ { 0 } ; m = m _ { 0 }$ is true, 

$$
P (X _ {k} <   m _ {0}) = P (X _ {k} > m _ {0}) = \frac {1}{2}, \qquad k = 1, 2, \ldots , n.
$$

Hence, the probability is $1 / 2$ that a negative sign is associated with the rank $R _ { k }$ of $| X _ { k } \mathrm { ~ - ~ } m _ { 0 } |$ . Moreover, the assignments of these n signs are independent because $X _ { 1 } , X _ { 2 } , \ldots , X _ { n }$ are mutually independent. In addition, W is a sum that contains the integers $1 , 2 , \ldots , n ,$ , each with a positive or negative sign. Because the underlying distribution is symmetric, it seems intuitively obvious that W has the same distribution as the random variable 

$$
V = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} V _ {k},
$$

where $V _ { 1 } , V _ { 2 } , \dots , V _ { n }$ are independent and 

$$
P (V _ {k} = k) = P (V _ {k} = - k) = \frac {1}{2}, \qquad k = 1, 2, \ldots , n.
$$

That is, V is a sum that contains the integers $1 , 2 , \ldots , n .$ , and these integers receive their algebraic signs by independent assignments. 

Because W and V have the same distribution, their means and variances are equal, and we can easily find those of V. Now, the mean of $V _ { k }$ is 

$$
E (V _ {k}) = - k \left(\frac {1}{2}\right) + k \left(\frac {1}{2}\right) = 0;
$$

thus, 

$$
E (W) = E (V) = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} E (V _ {k}) = 0.
$$

The variance of $V _ { k }$ is 

$$
\operatorname{Var} \left(V _ {k}\right) = E \left(V _ {k} ^ {2}\right) = (- k) ^ {2} \left(\frac {1}{2}\right) + (k) ^ {2} \left(\frac {1}{2}\right) = k ^ {2}.
$$

Hence, 

$$
\operatorname{Var} (W) = \operatorname{Var} (V) = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} \operatorname{Var} (V _ {k}) = \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {n} k ^ {2} = \frac {n (n + 1) (2 n + 1)}{6}.
$$

We shall not try to find the distribution of W in general because that pmf does not have a convenient expression. However, we demonstrate how we could find the distribution of W (or V) with enough patience and computer support. Recall that the moment-generating function of $V _ { k }$ is 

$$
M _ {k} (t) = e ^ {t (- k)} \left(\frac {1}{2}\right) + e ^ {t (+ k)} \left(\frac {1}{2}\right) = \frac {e ^ {- k t} + e ^ {k t}}{2}, \quad k = 1, 2, \dots , n, \quad - \infty <   t <   \infty .
$$

Let $n = 2 ;$ then the moment-generating function of $V _ { 1 } + V _ { 2 }$ is 

$$
M (t) = E [ e ^ {t (V _ {1} + V _ {2})} ], \qquad - \infty <   t <   \infty .
$$

From the independence of $V _ { 1 }$ and $V _ { 2 }$ , we obtain 

$$
\begin{array}{l} M (t) = E (e ^ {t V _ {1}}) E (e ^ {t V _ {2}}) \\ \qquad = \bigg (\frac {e ^ {- t} + e ^ {t}}{2} \bigg) \bigg (\frac {e ^ {- 2 t} + e ^ {2 t}}{2} \bigg) \\ \qquad = \frac {e ^ {- 3 t} + e ^ {- t} + e ^ {t} + e ^ {3 t}}{4}, \qquad - \infty <   t <   \infty . \end{array}
$$

This means that each of the points $- 3 , - 1 , 1 , 3$ in the support of $V _ { 1 } + V _ { 2 }$ has probability $1 / 4$ 

Next let $n = 3 ;$ then the moment-generating function of $V _ { 1 } + V _ { 2 } + V _ { 3 }$ is 

$$
\begin{array}{l} M (t) = E [ e ^ {t (V _ {1} + V _ {2} + V _ {3})} ] \\ \quad = E [ e ^ {t (V _ {1} + V _ {2})} ] E (e ^ {t V _ {3}}) \\ \quad = \bigg (\frac {e ^ {- 3 t} + e ^ {- t} + e ^ {t} + e ^ {3 t}}{4} \bigg) \bigg (\frac {e ^ {- 3 t} + e ^ {3 t}}{2} \bigg) \\ \quad = \frac {e ^ {- 6 t} + e ^ {- 4 t} + e ^ {- 2 t} + 2 e ^ {0} + e ^ {- 2 t} + e ^ {- 4 t} + e ^ {- 6 t}}{8}, \qquad - \infty <   t <   \infty . \end{array}
$$

Thus, the points $- 6 , - 4 , - 2 , 0 , 2 , 4 .$ , and 6 in the support of $V _ { 1 } + V _ { 2 } + V _ { 3 }$ have the respective probabilities $1 / 8 , 1 / 8 , 1 / 8 , 2 / 8 , 1 / 8 , 1 / 8 .$ and $1 / 8 .$ Obviously, this procedure can be continued for $n \ = \ 4 , 5 , 6 , \ldots .$ , but it is rather tedious. Fortunately, however, even though $V _ { 1 } , V _ { 2 } , \dots , V _ { n }$ are not identically distributed random variables, the sum V of them still has an approximate normal distribution. To obtain this normal approximation for V (or W), a more general form of the central limit theorem than the one proved in Section 5.9 can be used that allows us to say that the standardized random variable

(a) n = 4

(b) n = 10



Figure 8.5-1 The Wilcoxon distribution


$$
Z = \frac {W - 0}{\sqrt {n (n + 1) (2 n + 1) / 6}}
$$

is approximately $N ( 0 , 1 )$ when $H _ { 0 }$ is true. We accept this more general central limit theorem without proof so that we can use a normal distribution to approximate probabilities such as $P ( W \geq c ; H _ { 0 } ) \approx P ( Z \geq z _ { \alpha } ; H _ { 0 } )$ when the sample size n is sufficiently large, where c is a specified constant. The next example illustrates this approximation. 

The moment-generating function of W or of V is given by 

$$
M (t) = \prod_ {k = 1} ^ {n} \frac {e ^ {- k t} + e ^ {k t}}{2}, \qquad - \infty <   t <   \infty .
$$

Using a computer algebra system such as Maple, we can expand M(t) and find the coefficients of $e ^ { k t }$ , which is equal to $P ( W \ = \ k )$ . In Figure 8.5-1, we have drawn a probability histogram for the distribution of W along with the approximating $N [ 0 , n ( n + 1 ) ( 2 n + 1 ) / 6 ]$ pdf for $n = 4$ (a poor approximation) and for $n = 1 0$ It is important to note that the widths of the rectangles in the probability histogram are equal to 2, so the “half-unit correction for continuity” mentioned in Section 5.7 now is equal to 1. 

Let m be the median of a symmetric distribution of the continuous type. To test the hypothesis $H _ { 0 } ; m = 1 6 0$ against the alternative hypothesis $H _ { 1 } \colon m > 1 6 0$ , we take a random sample of size $n = 1 6 $ . Say the observed values of the sample are 176.9, 158.3, 152.1, 158.8, 172.4, 169.8, 159.7, 162.7, 156.6, 174.5, 184.4, 165.2, 147.8, 177.8, 160.1, and 160.5. In Table 8.5-1, the magnitudes of the differences $\lvert x _ { k } - 1 6 0 \rvert$ have been ordered and ranked. Those differences $x _ { k } - 1 6 0$ that were negative have been underlined, and the ranks are under the ordered values. For this set of data, 

$$
w = 1 - 2 + 3 - 4 - 5 + 6 + \dots + 1 6 = 6 0.
$$
